headline: Reporter says lengthy Texas execution was ‘like no other’ he’d seen
author: Victoria Craw

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering breaking news from London

Texas prisoner Reinaldo Dennes cried out in pain as he was executed Thursday, in a procedure that extended over an hour as staff struggled to find veins suitable for intravenous needles, the Associated Press reported.
Dennes, 70, faced the death penalty for a 1996 murder and robbery, according to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.

Associated Press reporter Michael Graczyk, who witnessed the execution in Huntsville, said it was “dramatically different” from the hundreds of other executions he had witnessed. In Texas, access to witness death penalty proceedings is tightly controlled.

Once a lethal dose of pentobarbital had been delivered, Graczyk said, Dennes “moaned in excruciating pain” for almost three minutes, crying out, asking God to take him, and at one point saying: “I don’t think this is normal.” The execution was “like no other” he had witnessed before, Graczyk added.

Prison officials said the correct procedures were followed and suggested Dennes was “exaggerating or even faking his pain,” Graczyk said. The Texas Department of Criminal Justice did not immediately reply to an overnight request for comment.
The death penalty, particularly death by lethal injection, has been the spotlight since the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September.
Reporter covering international breaking news
Four men guilty of assaulting woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
Four British men have been convicted of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged her and invited strangers online to use her for sex, in the first case of its kind to go to trial in England.
Joanne Young, who waived her right to anonymity, told reporters after the trial ended Thursday: “The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.”
Philip Young, 50, whom she divorced last year, pleaded guilty to multiple sexual offenses in January.

Young, who served as a Conservative local government councillor in the town of Swindon between 2007 and 2010, was caught after police discovered he uploaded extreme bestiality images online. Police then uncovered other images, including of Joanne Young being raped.
A sixth man pleaded guilty to rape and assault before the trial began.

The couple’s daughter has called for a change in England’s consent laws, writing: “We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone … This is simply unacceptable.”
The case had echoes of that of Gisèle Pelicot in France. Her then-husband was found guilty of repeatedly drugging and raping his wife and orchestrating her abuse by dozens of men.
Owl survives 45-mile drive stuck to front of truck after collision

Ashley Moffitt was driving on a Pennsylvania highway recently when an owl collided with the front of her freight truck. It wasn’t until she arrived at her destination about 45 miles away that she saw the owl’s head was trapped above the windshield.
Somehow, the owl was alive.
“When you’re going 65 miles an hour and it hits, I honestly didn’t think that anything like that could survive,” said Moffitt, a line-haul driver for Old Dominion Freight Line.
Employees from the freight company removed the owl, which had been stuck in a fiberglass panel, and called a wildlife rehabilitation center that night, Nov. 6.
Tracie Young, founder of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in Washington Boro, Pennsylvania, said she struggled to believe the owl was alive until she saw photos of him standing.
“How he didn’t break his neck is just beyond me,” Young said. “I have honestly never heard of a bird of prey even surviving that.”

If birds do survive car collisions, Young said, they’re typically severely injured. When wildlife rehabilitators inspected the great horned owl that night, Young said, his only injury was damage to his left eye, which was swollen and bleeding.

The owl, which Young said was probably born this year, is recovering at the center. When the owl shows he can fly and forage on his own, Young said, the center will release him in Franklin County, near where he collided with Moffitt’s truck.
Reporter covering brain health and writer of the Brain Matters column
Video games like ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ may have surprising brain benefits

“Grand Theft Auto VI” has taken the world by storm. Many people are reportedly taking time off from their jobs to immerse themselves in the crime epic. In doing so, they may actually be putting their brains to work.

Researchers have found that action video games similar to “Grand Theft Auto VI” may help improve cognitive skills by challenging the brain to make split-second decisions. A 2022 study reported that people who played at least five hours of action video games a week — including previous editions of “Grand Theft Auto” — performed better than non-gamers at a task that involved mentally visualizing rotating objects.

In another study, scientists had non-gamers play action video games about five hours a week for three months. By the end of the study, the participants had boosted their learning speed. They picked up two unrelated skills faster than people who played a slower type of game.
But of course, moderation is key.

“I cannot say that playing video games for hours and hours and hours is going to be good for your brain health,” Carlos Coronel, a research fellow at Trinity College Dublin and Adolfo Ibañez University in Santiago, Chile, previously told me. “You need to find a balance.”
Agriculture Secretary’s religious emails are unconstitutional, judge rules

A federal judge ruled Thursday that religious messages Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins sent to her department amount to a violation of the Constitution, stressing that “the Secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages.”

The case, filed by a labor union and six employees, took issue with emails Rollins sent, particularly a Christmas video message and an Easter message of several paragraphs that was sent to about 100,000 USDA employees.

“Happy Easter — He is Risen indeed! Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind,” Rollins wrote in the email, which was reviewed by The Washington Post. Several employees told The Post the message unnerved them, and legal experts said the message defied a norm of officials steering clear of overtly religious language.

Judge Trina L. Thompson in California said Rollins’s emails breached the establishment clause of the Constitution, designed to prevent the government from influencing a person’s faith, and USDA’s own rules, given Rollins’s position of authority, the use of her official email and language alienating to those who did not share her beliefs.
A USDA spokesperson called the ruling an “unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary.”
Columnist covering food and nutrition
Try this simple swap for better sleep over the holidays
Thanksgiving is a time to indulge, and for many people, that includes enjoying more than their fair share of wine, beer or cocktails.
If Thanksgiving typically turns into Drinksgiving for you, doing so could have a dramatic impact on your sleep.

In studies, scientists have found that regularly drinking alcohol — even one to two drinks a day — can worsen your sleep, leading to a higher likelihood of snoring, staying up late and difficulty getting up in the morning. But studies have shown that reducing your alcohol intake can lead to better sleep, reductions in blood pressure and body weight, and other health benefits.

That’s because alcohol is a double-edged sword when it comes to sleep. It acts as a sedative that can help you fall asleep faster. But as your body metabolizes alcohol through the night, you’ll experience more light sleep, leading to more arousals and awakenings. Alcohol also relaxes the muscles in your throat that keep your airway open, leading to snoring and disrupted breathing.

For better sleep, consider using nonalcoholic wines, beers and spirits as substitutes for alcoholic beverages, or at least to reduce or moderate your alcohol intake. Many bars and restaurants serve them, and they can be especially helpful if you feel pressure to drink in social settings, especially during the holidays.
Or consider trying a new mocktail recipe. To get you started, here are seven Washington Post recipes for fun and delicious mocktails you can make at home.
